paragraphs.heading: Built in layers
paragraphs.text: A stratovolcano is a typically cone-shaped volcano made of many alternating layers, or strata, of hardened lava and tephra. Its other name, composite volcano, is used because the strata are usually mixed and uneven, not neat layers. Stratovolcanoes are among the most common types of volcano. More than 700 of them have erupted lava during the last 11,700 years.

paragraphs.heading: Where they form
paragraphs.text: Stratovolcanoes are typically found at subduction zones. There they form chains and clusters along plate boundaries where a plate of oceanic crust is drawn under a plate of continental crust, as in the Andes, or under another plate of oceanic crust, as in Japan. They occur in some other settings too. Teide in the Canary Islands is an example from an oceanic island far from plate boundaries. Stratovolcanoes have also formed in continental rifts.

paragraphs.heading: How the magma is made
paragraphs.text: Subduction zone volcanoes form when hydrous minerals are carried down into the mantle on the slab. Chlorite and serpentine are examples. They give up their water to the mantle, and that lowers its melting point by 60 to 100 °C. The mantle can then partly melt and generate magma. The magma rises through the crust and takes in silica-rich crustal rock on the way. When it nears the top, it pools in a magma chamber inside the crust, beneath the stratovolcano.

paragraphs.heading: What sets off an eruption
paragraphs.text: Several things can raise the pressure in the chamber. The lightest magma, which is the richest in silica, and volatiles such as water and sulfur dioxide can gather in the top of the chamber, which can dramatically increase pressures. Minerals such as feldspar can crystallize out of the magma, which concentrates volatiles in the liquid that is left and can lead a gas to separate from it. Fresh magma can be injected into the chamber, where it mixes with and heats the cooler magma already there. These internal triggers may be modified by external ones such as earthquakes or interactions with groundwater.

paragraphs.heading: Why the eruptions are explosive
paragraphs.text: Lava from a stratovolcano has high viscosity, and it typically cools and hardens before spreading far. Subduction-zone stratovolcanoes typically erupt explosively, because the magma is too viscous to let volcanic gases escape easily. The pressure of the trapped gases stays inside the pasty magma. Once the vent is breached and the crater opens, the magma degasses explosively, and magma and gases blast out at high speed.

paragraphs.heading: The human cost
paragraphs.text: In recorded history, explosive eruptions at subduction zone volcanoes have posed the greatest hazard to civilizations. Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883, claiming 36,000 lives. Mount Vesuvius in Italy erupted in 79 A.D. and killed an estimated 2,000 people. Volcanic eruptions have killed nearly 300,000 people since 1600 CE.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond Earth
paragraphs.text: Whether stratovolcanoes exist on other Solar System bodies has not been conclusively shown. Two mountains in the Aeolis region of Mars have been proposed as possible stratovolcanoes, and Zephyria Tholus is one of them.
